subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE Eduqas Biology simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: Trophic levels and pyramids of biomass

questions.q: An ecosystem is best defined as:
options: The interaction of a community of living organisms with the non-living parts of their environment
All the members of one species in an area
Only the plants in a habitat
questions.explain: An ecosystem is the interaction of a community of living (biotic) organisms with the non-living (abiotic) parts of their environment. A community is all the populations in an area.

questions.q: All the organisms of the SAME species living in a habitat form a:
questions.explain: A population is all the organisms of one species in a habitat. A community is all the different populations together; the ecosystem includes these plus abiotic factors.

questions.q: Which of these is an ABIOTIC factor in an ecosystem?
questions.explain: Abiotic (non-living) factors include light intensity, temperature, moisture, soil pH and mineral content. Predators, food availability and disease are biotic (living) factors.

questions.q: Which is a BIOTIC factor that could reduce the size of a rabbit population?
options: An increase in the number of foxes (predators)
questions.explain: Biotic factors are living factors. More predators (foxes) is a biotic factor reducing the rabbit population. Temperature, pH and light are abiotic factors.

questions.q: Within a community, organisms depend on each other for resources. This is called:
questions.explain: Interdependence means organisms rely on one another for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal. Removing one species can affect many others in the community.

questions.q: Two plant species growing close together are most likely to compete for:
questions.explain: Plants compete for light, water, space and mineral ions. Animals compete for food, mates, water and territory. Competition limits population size.

questions.q: In a food chain, what is a producer?
options: An organism that eats other animals
An organism (usually a green plant or alga) that makes its own food by photosynthesis
questions.explain: A producer makes its own organic material, usually by photosynthesis (green plants and algae). Producers start almost all food chains, capturing light energy.

questions.q: In the chain: grass -> rabbit -> fox, the rabbit is the:
questions.explain: The rabbit eats the producer (grass), so it is the primary consumer (herbivore). The fox, which eats the rabbit, is the secondary consumer.

questions.q: If disease killed most of the rabbits in a food web, the number of foxes would most likely:
options: Decrease, as they have less food
questions.explain: Foxes depend on rabbits for food, so fewer rabbits means the fox population would fall. This shows the interdependence of organisms in a food web.

questions.lo: Trophic levels and pyramids of biomass
questions.q: A trophic level describes:
options: The position (feeding level) of an organism in a food chain
The number of species in an area
questions.explain: A trophic level is the position an organism occupies in a food chain (e.g. producer, primary consumer). Pyramids of biomass show the biomass at each trophic level.

questions.lo: Trophic levels and pyramids of biomass
questions.q: A pyramid of biomass shows:
options: The number of organisms at each level
The dry mass of living material at each trophic level
questions.explain: A pyramid of biomass represents the mass of living material (biomass) at each trophic level. It is almost always pyramid-shaped because biomass decreases up the chain.

questions.q: Only about 10% of biomass is passed to the next trophic level. Where does most of the rest go?
options: It is lost through respiration, movement, and as waste (faeces/urine) and uneaten parts
It is stored as starch in predators
questions.explain: Biomass and energy are lost at each level through respiration (heat), movement, egestion (faeces) and excretion, and because not all parts are eaten. This limits food chain length.

questions.q: (Higher tier) 10,000 kJ of biomass is available in producers. If 10% transfers each level, roughly how much reaches the secondary consumers?
questions.explain: 10% of 10,000 = 1000 kJ reaches primary consumers; 10% of 1000 = 100 kJ reaches secondary consumers. Efficiency = (biomass after / biomass before) x 100.

questions.q: In the carbon cycle, carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere by:
questions.explain: Photosynthesis removes CO2 from the atmosphere, fixing carbon into glucose. Respiration, combustion and decomposition return CO2 to the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which TWO processes return carbon dioxide to the atmosphere?
questions.explain: Respiration by living organisms and combustion of fossil fuels/wood both release CO2 back to the atmosphere. Decomposition also releases CO2.

questions.q: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi are important because they:
options: Produce their own food by photosynthesis
Break down dead organisms and waste, recycling mineral ions to the soil
questions.explain: Decomposers break down dead organisms and waste, releasing carbon dioxide and returning mineral ions (e.g. nitrates) to the soil for plants to reuse - recycling materials.

questions.q: Which conditions generally give the FASTEST rate of decomposition?
questions.explain: Decomposition is fastest in warm, moist, well-oxygenated (aerobic) conditions, which suit decomposer microorganisms and their enzymes. Waterlogged, cold or acidic conditions slow it.

questions.q: A quadrat is used to:
options: Sample and estimate the abundance/distribution of organisms in a known area
questions.explain: A quadrat is a square frame of known area used to sample the number/distribution of (usually) plants or slow-moving animals, allowing an estimate of the whole population.

questions.q: To study how a plant species changes across a field from a hedge, a student should use a:
questions.explain: A transect is a line along which samples (quadrats) are taken at intervals. It is used to measure how the distribution of organisms changes across a gradient (e.g. from a hedge).

questions.q: Biodiversity is:
options: The variety of different species of organisms in an ecosystem or on Earth
The number of one species in an area
questions.explain: Biodiversity is the variety of species in an ecosystem or on Earth. High biodiversity makes ecosystems more stable. Human activities (deforestation, pollution) can reduce it.
